title: Tree of Coprimes
spaceBreakdown:
- vector<vector<int>> adj: n vectors with 2(n-1) total ints → O(n)
- bool cop[51][51]: fixed 2601 bools → O(1)
- vector<int> ans: n ints (returned output, not counted)
- vector<vector<pair<int,int>>> stacks: 50 vectors, total entries ≤ tree height h at any time → O(h) ≤ O(n)
- vector<array<int,4>> stk (explicit DFS stack): worst case O(n) entries (e.g., star graph) → O(n)
- not counted: input nums/edges, returned ans
approach: Since values are ≤ 50, keep one stack per value holding (depth, node) of ancestors currently on the root path. During DFS, when entering a node, scan all 50 values coprime with its value and take the deepest stack top - that is the closest coprime ancestor. Push the node onto its value's stack on entry and pop it on exit, so stacks always mirror the current root-to-node path. Correctness: for each value only the deepest (closest) ancestor on the path can be the answer, and the coprime table is precomputed once.
hints: A node can have up to 10^5 ancestors, yet each value is between 1 and 50. Along the root path, among ancestors sharing the same value, which one is the only candidate worth comparing?

Keep one stack per value (1-50) of (depth, node) for ancestors on the current root path. In Example 1, when node 3 (value 2) is entered, the value-3 stack top is (depth 1, node 1) and gcd(2,3)=1, so the answer is node 1, beating the deeper... shallower value-2 entry (depth 0, node 0).

precompute cop[a][b] = (gcd(a,b)==1) for a,b in 1..50
iterative DFS from root, frames carry (node, parent, depth, exitFlag)
on enter u:
    best = deepest top among stacks v with cop[nums[u]][v] and stack nonempty
    ans[u] = best's node (or -1)
    push (depth, u) onto stack[nums[u]]
    push exit frame; push children with depth+1
on exit u:
    pop stack[nums[u]]

Single node - no edges at all, no ancestors exist.
`Input: nums = [7], edges = []` → `Expected: [-1]`
⚠️ Bug: assuming edges has at least one element or returning 0 for the root → returns [0] instead of [-1].

All values equal and > 1 - no node is coprime with its own value repeated down the path.
`Input: nums = [2,2,2], edges = [[0,1],[1,2]]` → `Expected: [-1,-1,-1]`
⚠️ Bug: skipping the gcd check for equal values (assuming same value means "already handled") → returns [-1,0,0].

Chain of value 1 - gcd(1,1)=1, so every node's parent is a valid answer.
`Input: nums = [1,1,1], edges = [[0,1],[1,2]]` → `Expected: [-1,0,1]`
⚠️ Bug: a coprime table that marks cop[1][1] = false → returns [-1,-1,0].

Skewed tree of 10^5 nodes - recursion depth hits 10^5.
`Input: nums = [1]*100000, edges = [[i,i+1] for i in 0..99998]` → `Expected: [-1,0,1,...,99998]`
⚠️ Bug: recursive DFS without raising the stack limit → stack overflow / runtime error; use an explicit stack.

Sibling subtrees must not see each other - a finished subtree's entries must be popped before an uncle node is processed.
`Input: nums = [5,6,10,3], edges = [[0,1],[0,2],[1,3]]` → `Expected: [-1,0,-1,0]`
⚠️ Bug: pushing ancestor entries without popping on exit → node 2 (value 10) wrongly sees node 3 (value 3) and returns 3 instead of -1.

followUps.q: What if values could be up to 10^9 instead of 50?
followUps.a: The per-value stack trick dies; instead factor each value and keep, for each prime, the deepest ancestor divisible by it. A node's answer is the closest ancestor sharing no prime factor, found by taking the maximum depth over primes NOT dividing it - still O(n log V) per query overall with O(n · ω(V)) space.

followUps.q: What if you must answer queries "closest coprime ancestor of node u with value constraint" online after the tree is built?
followUps.a: Preprocess with the same DFS, but persist the 50 stacks as persistent arrays (one version per root-path prefix), giving O(1) query per node after O(50·n) preprocessing and O(50·n) space. Alternatively use binary lifting with per-value jump tables for O(log n) queries.

followUps.q: What if memory is limited to O(50) beyond the tree and recursion?
followUps.a: You cannot store per-node answers during one pass, but you can still answer everything in O(50·n) time with O(h) extra space: the per-value stacks themselves only hold the current path (≤ h entries across all 50 stacks), so the algorithm above already achieves this if you drop the adjacency list in favor of a parent array plus child iteration by edge index.
